title: AI simulation: Practice substitutes remain unvalidated
desc: Proposes realistic scenarios and feedback to replace lost experience while preserving structured teaching, mentoring and consequential judgment.

kps.k: AI simulation offers a proposed replacement for lost practice opportunities, not a replacement for lawyers’ judgment.
kps.d: Runyon argues that automation removes foundational assignments before juniors develop experience-based judgment. Daves and AltaClaro frame repeatable rehearsal as a way to give associates earlier practice without exposing clients to training mistakes. This responds both to anticipated automation and to longstanding problems: scarce deposition opportunities, costly exercises and uneven access to meaningful assignments. Claims that simulation will accelerate professional development remain predictions.

qs.q: Now, as AI takes over these foundational tasks, that *repetition loop* is breaking down, according to [a new report](https://www.positivegroup.org/loop/reports/the-ai-leadership-challenge-in-law/), which underscores how junior lawyers are being thrust into higher-level advisory work far earlier in their careers.
qs.a: How AI Simulation Could Reshape Legal Training and Education · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: “It fills a crucial gap that traditional, costly, and infrequent deposition training models simply cannot address.”  AltaClaro frames DepoSim within its broader philosophy of Deliberate Practice – the principle, borrowed from sports and performing arts, that skills are built through repeated, feedback-intensive repetition rather than passive observation or one-time exposure.
qs.a: AltaClaro and Verbit Launch DepoSim, an AI-Powered Deposition Simulator for Litigators · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The proposed learning mechanism combines realistic decisions, variable scenarios and specific feedback.
kps.d: Runyon recommends clear learning goals, controlled unpredictability and feedback tied to judgment calls, with usability determining whether lawyers practise. DepoSim and Stanford liftlab vary witness behavior to force adaptation rather than script-following. Ambrogi’s DepoSim demonstration showed live spoken exchanges, objections and prompt feedback linked to transcript passages. These observations establish functionality, not the accuracy of every assessment or transfer of learning to client work.

qs.q: AI simulation — if designed with enough precision to force real decision-making — can create the repetitive environments in which that judgment can be developed.
qs.a: How AI Simulation Could Reshape Legal Training and Education · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: For each category, the feedback identifies what went well, what needed improvement, and how to improve, along with specific transcript references, citing the point in the transcript where a particular issue arose.
qs.a: AltaClaro and Verbit Launch DepoSim, an AI-Powered Deposition Simulator for Litigators · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Early deployment shows adoption and favorable reactions, but does not establish improved advocacy.
kps.d: Campisi reports DepoSim adoption at Orrick, Taft, Brownstein and Littler, including favorable responses from Brownstein’s nine-lawyer pilot and increased peer engagement at Orrick. Ambrogi reports a five-week beta involving six Am Law 100 firms: the companies claimed more than 160 testing hours, 97% strong agreement that the tool was valuable and 94% willingness to reuse it. These are satisfaction measures and reported experiences, not comparative learning outcomes. Repeated vendor testimonials and AltaClaro’s accompanying promotional summary do not independently corroborate effectiveness.

qs.q: Law firms including Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe, Taft Stettinius & Hollister, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck and Littler Mendelson have all incorporated an AI-powered deposition simulator for associate training.
qs.a: A Different Kind of Pilot: Deposition Simulator Emerges as a Training Tool for Big Law Associates · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: According to the companies, participants logged more than 160 hours of testing, and 97% strongly agreed that DepoSim is valuable for litigation training, while 94% said they would use it again.
qs.a: AltaClaro and Verbit Launch DepoSim, an AI-Powered Deposition Simulator for Litigators · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The central disagreement concerns how much simulation can substitute for consequential experience.
kps.d: The Training Crisis argues that real deadlines, client stakes and partner criticism teach differently from consequence-free exercises and AI scoring. Its pilot-training analogy supports a mixed model conceptually, not empirically. Yet it does not defend existing apprenticeship: it questions repetitive document review’s demonstrated training value and partners’ ability to distribute opportunities equitably. The debate therefore concerns the right combination of simulation, mentorship and supervised work, rather than a binary choice between technology and apprenticeship.

qs.q: The pressure of real consequences sharpens attention in ways that practice exercises may not.
qs.a: The Training Crisis · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Nor are we saying that the current modes of apprenticeship training are necessary, or even particularly effective at producing deep domain expertise.
qs.a: The Training Crisis · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Practical implementation centers on structured teaching and mentoring, not simply distributing software.
kps.d: Reported uses include partner demonstrations, paired practice, mentor review and preparation for upcoming depositions; experienced litigators also use rehearsal to refresh skills. Daves describes DepoSim as supplemental training. Runyon advocates curricular integration and strategic training infrastructure, while Campisi places Orrick’s adoption alongside protected early-career training time. Shayesteh also distinguishes collaborative coaching from mandatory sharing: he says learners can choose whether to share session records with mentors.

qs.q: "It is really a supplement [to] training programs that we are already doing to give associates experience that they would not otherwise have," she said.
qs.a: A Different Kind of Pilot: Deposition Simulator Emerges as a Training Tool for Big Law Associates · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Also, mentor-mentee pairs are using the tool’s embedded feedback as the foundation for coaching conversations; and associates with upcoming real depositions are using the tool for targeted preparation.
qs.a: How AI Simulation Could Reshape Legal Training and Education · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Simulation could broaden access to rehearsal, but advocacy types require distinct training assumptions.
kps.d: McCormack draws on judicial experience to propose practice tools for solos, small-firm lawyers and advocates without colleagues to moot cases. Leonard proposes tailored negotiation scenarios and analysis of AI-generated arguments, while leaving open how written persuasion differs from live advocacy involving interaction and nonverbal communication. These proposals extend the theme beyond large-firm associate development; they do not demonstrate AI’s persuasive superiority or improved outcomes for under-resourced clients.

qs.q: For lawyers in small firms, solos, or those assigned to high-stakes cases like termination of parental rights without institutional support — they often didn’t have anyone to moot with.
qs.a: Can AI Be More Persuasive Than a Human Lawyer? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: But with this technology, they could build a tool, practice with it, and get real-time feedback on each persuasive move they try.
qs.a: Can AI Be More Persuasive Than a Human Lawyer? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Broader simulations and economic benefits remain a development agenda rather than established results.
kps.d: Harvey’s Gabe Pereyra proposes capturing firm expertise and building end-to-end simulated mergers, litigation and fund formation, with feedback from simulated clients and partners. He envisages infrastructure that trains both humans and agents, grounding faster-learning expectations in intuition about low-value repetition. AltaClaro plans additional advocacy and negotiation scenarios and forecasts real-case simulation. Its leaders also predict lower training costs and more efficient client work, but the supplied evidence contains no quantified savings or tested end-to-end educational outcomes.

qs.q: The first step is putting all the feedback, all the practice guides, all of that institutional knowledge into these systems so they can be used to train associates.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: And eventually the technology is there, especially in our partnership with Verbit, where, by next year, we’ll be able to simulate real cases.
qs.a: The Flight Simulator for Lawyers: Abdi Shayesteh and Jeanine Conley Daves on AI, Deliberate Practice, and the Future of Legal Training · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: These selected market-analyst, consultancy and press sources accept the proposition that AI simulation can restore some practice opportunities lost or made scarce by automation, cost and limited access to live matters, while remaining a supplement to—not a replacement for—human judgment, structured teaching and mentoring. Collectively, they materially develop the proposition by specifying a learning model: repeated decision-making under variable, realistic conditions; prompt, rubric-based feedback tied to particular performance moments; and integration into partner demonstrations, mentor coaching and preparation for real depositions. There is meaningful internal variation in emphasis. Runyon advances the broadest normative and pedagogical argument, including design principles and curricular integration. Ambrogi concentrates on demonstrated product functionality and company-reported beta reactions. Campisi emphasizes law-firm adoption, safe practice and placement within wider professional-development programs. Across these accounts, favorable reactions, engagement and willingness to reuse the tool are distinguished from validated learning outcomes: none supplies comparative evidence that simulation improves advocacy, transfers reliably to consequential client work or fully substitutes for experience under real stakes. The position therefore builds on the cluster’s cautious proposition without resolving its central validation gap. Because the corpus is curated, this synthesis characterizes only these sources and does not indicate the prevalence of this view among market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

qs.q: AI simulation — if designed with enough precision to force real decision-making — can create the repetitive environments in which that judgment can be developed.

vlens.an: The curated sources assigned to this professional voice accept the cluster’s principal proposition that AI simulation can supplement lost or scarce practice opportunities while remaining unvalidated as a substitute for consequential experience and professional judgment. They materially extend it in two directions. Pereyra proposes firm-specific systems that combine institutional knowledge with end-to-end simulated matters and feedback from simulated clients and partners, potentially training both junior lawyers and AI agents. Leonard and McCormack broaden the application beyond large-firm associate development to negotiation, persuasion and advocacy rehearsal, particularly for solos, small-firm lawyers and advocates without colleagues or institutional support. Their common rationale is that repeatable, tailored practice and immediate feedback could provide experience that is otherwise scarce, costly or unevenly distributed. Material variation concerns the setting and learning assumptions: Pereyra emphasises institutional knowledge and whole-matter simulation, whereas Leonard and McCormack emphasise access to advocacy rehearsal and distinguish written persuasion from live oral advocacy. Across both sources, claimed benefits are proposals, predictions or personal observations rather than measured improvements in learning or client outcomes, which reinforces rather than resolves the cluster’s validation caveat.

qs.q: You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: But with this technology, they could build a tool, practice with it, and get real-time feedback on each persuasive move they try.
qs.a: Can AI Be More Persuasive Than a Human Lawyer? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI simulation should supplement, rather than wholly replace, consequential practice, structured teaching and mentorship. Its main reason is that live client stakes, real deadlines and consequential errors create learning conditions that simulated exercises and AI scoring may not reproduce. At the same time, it does not defend traditional apprenticeship as inherently effective: repetitive junior work may have weak training value, and partner-led allocation of meaningful assignments can be uneven. The source therefore endorses a mixed model combining simulation, deliberate mentorship, real-world exposure and AI-assisted feedback if junior work contracts. Material variation lies in its dual skepticism toward both simulation-only training and the existing apprenticeship model. Its proposed combination is conceptual and analogy-based rather than empirically validated, aligning with the cluster’s caution that practice substitutes remain unproven. Because this facet contains one curated source, the finding characterises that source rather than academia and research generally.

qs.q: Instead, the question is what combination --- accelerated simulations, deliberate mentorship, real-world exposure, AI-assisted feedback --- can produce sufficient domain expertise in a sufficient number of junior lawyers if the volume of traditional junior work shrinks.
qs.a: The Training Crisis · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The legal-tech vendor source supports the proposition that AI simulation can compensate for lost or uneven practice opportunities while preserving human judgment, structured teaching and mentoring. It presents safe rehearsal on realistic assignments, rubric-based feedback and collaborative review as complements to apprenticeship rather than substitutes for lawyers. Material variation lies in the breadth and certainty of its claims: reported adoption, realism and positive reactions provide evidence of use and acceptance, but claims that simulation will accelerate skill development, equalise capability or produce client efficiencies remain forecasts rather than measured outcomes. The source also extends use beyond junior development to experienced litigators and envisages broader advocacy and real-case simulations, though these are deployment plans rather than validation. Because this is one curated vendor source, its position should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: And that’s where I got the entrepreneurial bug again to launch AltaClaro, a place where attorneys can practice safely in simulated environments on assignments that are taken from the real world and get feedback.
qs.a: The Flight Simulator for Lawyers: Abdi Shayesteh and Jeanine Conley Daves on AI, Deliberate Practice, and the Future of Legal Training · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: How can we leverage it for those things that hopefully AI will never replace and build the human muscle for judgment?

elens.an: The 2025 source accepts the proposition’s core view that AI simulation can supplement missing practice opportunities while stopping short of claiming validated improvements in advocacy. It materially extends the proposition beyond large-firm associate training to solos, small-firm lawyers and advocates in high-stakes matters who lack colleagues or institutional support for mooting, proposing AI-enabled rehearsal with real-time feedback as a practical substitute for that missing access. It also broadens the training agenda from depositions to negotiation and persuasion, while introducing material internal variation: written advocacy may require different training and assessment from oral advocacy because it lacks live interaction and nonverbal communication. Claims that AI can generate superior arguments or deepen skills remain prospective and are not supported by measured educational or client outcomes.

qs.q: For lawyers in small firms, solos, or those assigned to high-stakes cases like termination of parental rights without institutional support — they often didn’t have anyone to moot with.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively support the proposition that AI simulation is a promising but still unvalidated substitute for some lost practice opportunities, and that it should augment rather than replace human judgment, mentoring and consequential experience. Their common rationale is that automation and uneven apprenticeship reduce junior lawyers’ repetitions, while realistic, variable scenarios and specific feedback can provide scalable, low-consequence rehearsal. Reported deployments demonstrate functionality, adoption and favorable participant reactions, but not comparative improvements in advocacy, judgment or transfer to client work. Material variation concerns the degree of substitution: product-oriented and implementation sources are more optimistic about accelerated learning, broader simulations and economic benefits, whereas The Training Crisis stresses that real stakes produce distinct learning and argues for an explicit combination of simulation, mentorship and supervised practice. Some sources also materially elaborate implementation through rubric-based feedback, mentor review and firm-specific end-to-end matters, but these extensions remain proposals or reported uses rather than validated outcomes.

qs.q: Instead, the question is what combination --- accelerated simulations, deliberate mentorship, real-world exposure, AI-assisted feedback --- can produce sufficient domain expertise in a sufficient number of junior lawyers if the volume of traditional junior work shrinks.
qs.a: The Training Crisis · Academia · 2026
